sections.title: The Meaning of the Service
sections.reading:
Almost 2,000 years ago, the story goes, a clutch of sleepy shepherds were watching over their sheep on a star- brightened hillside in Palestine. It was a still, uneventful night. Suddenly the darkness was filled with a strange light. The stillness was broken by angel voices singing “Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, goodwill to all.” So begins Christmas, a beautiful and meaningful celebration of the Christian calendar.

Christmas actually begins with Advent, the season through which we are moving. Advent means “coming”. We celebrate these days of Advent in expectation and preparation for Christ’s arrival. It proclaims the revelation of God’s love as expressed in Christ’s birth in a humble stable, His sacrificial death on the cross, and His victorious resurrection. It points to the hope of Christ’s coming again as the King of Kings and Lord of Lords. Advent makes innkeepers out of all of us, asking each of us to make room for the arrival of Christ the King. Let us, today, prepare Him room in our hearts, our lives, and our homes.

Both the seasons of Advent - the season of “going toward” the birth of Christ - and Christmas have a long history. These seasons and their customs have pagan origins but have been “converted” by redefining their meanings. What is significant for us is not what they may once have meant but rather what they mean for us today.

This evening our church building will begin to wear its Christmas apparel. For the first time our Christmas tree stands in the sanctuary. This day for the first time its lights will shine for us. As we make ready for the birth of the child by preparing this sanctuary, we make ready ourselves and the sanctuary of our own hearts. We are mindful that, although it is not Christmas yet, it will be here soon…. very soon.

As we decorate the church, not only will we explain the history of the symbols of these special seasons, but we will rededicate these symbols - and ourselves - to the service of God.

sections.title: The Christmas Tree
sections.reading:
There are several legends and stories about the Christmas tree. The first use of the Christmas tree was in the medieval German Paradise Plays, held outdoors and portraying the creation of humankind. In these plays, the Tree of Life was a fir tree decorated with apples. Later, other ornaments were hung upon them, such as paper flowers and gilded nuts. In England, branches or whole trees were forced into bloom indoors for Christmas. From these beginnings, the use of a tree at Christmas was established. Martin Luther was perhaps the first to use a lighted tree. The story is told that as he was walking home one Christmas Eve night, he looked up and saw stars shining through the branches of an evergreen tree reminding him of the radiant skies over Bethlehem on that glorious first Christmas Eve.  Wishing to share this beautiful picture with his wife and children, he cut an evergreen, glistening with snow, and took it home. He fastened candles on its branches, recreating the scene from outside.  The Christmas tree, decorated with lighted candles, soon became a permanent part of the Christmas celebration.

Today, the Christmas tree is the center of our festivities.  Glittering with lights and ornaments, it is part of the beauty and meaning of Christmas.  As we look at the tree itself, we see that the tree points upward.  This reminds us of Christ’s eternal home.  He was willing to humble Himself, to leave His home in glory, and to come to earth and become as we are to die on another tree for our sins.  We also see the green of the tree.  The evergreen, standing through the changing seasons, speaks of the unchanging eternal love of God and reminds us that we receive eternal life when we trust Jesus as Lord and Savior.

sections.title: The Chrismons
sections.reading:
Our Christmas tree will also be decorated with special ornaments called Chrismons.  Chrismons were first developed by Frances Kipps Spencer in 1957 when she set out to create decorations appropriate for a church Christmas tree.  They proclaim the name, the life, and the saving acts of Jesus Christ.  Some designs are simple copies of symbols of Christianity from its earliest days.  Others are new explanations of God’s constant presence in our ever-changing world, and some are combinations of several elements old and new.  Some may utilize only 1 or 2 elements to present their message, but most combine several signs, symbols, pictures, or types.  Designs differ in the way that they unite the various elements so that each Chrismon presents its unique message, but the basic signs and symbols remain the same.

All Chrismons are made in white or gold or in a combination of the two colors. White suggests the innocence, purity, and perfection of our Savior. In our culture, it’s the color of joy.  Gold is the symbol for the glory and majesty of God and the Son of God.

This year several of our church families were asked to make a Chrismon ornament to add to our Christmas tree. May these symbols continually remind us of God’s greatest gift of all - Jesus Christ.
sections.stageInstructions: As Cody plays, those who were enlisted to make Chrismons may bring them to the front and place them on the tree.

sections.title: The Sanctuary Greens
sections.reading:
We come to the sanctuary greens.  Many kinds of greenery are used to adorn the sanctuary at Christmastime.  The scent and color of the evergreens represent renewal, new life, freshness, and rebirth. Long before the birth of Jesus, evergreens were used as an emblem of eternal life. Now as a Christian symbol, the evergreen represents Jesus Christ, who is Himself eternal life.

The thorny leaves and red berries of the holly remind us of the crown of thorns Jesus wore when He was crucified and the drops of blood that He shed to atone for our sins.  One legend of the first Christmas states that as the shepherds went to the manger, a little lamb following them was scratched by holly thorns. The red berries are drops of blood that froze on the holly branches. Long ago, Christians placed this reminder of the gift of Christ’s life in their windows to indicate that He had entered their home.

Ivy too, is rich in symbolism. In the Middle Ages, ivy was used extensively for Christmas decorating. It was considered a symbol of love because of its clinging habit of growth. Holly and ivy are often associated together in legend because both have the incredible ability to survive and grow.

Pine, fir, and cedar symbolize life and immortality. In addition to that, cedar also symbolizes strength, excellence, and endurance. It was used for purification. We use it as a sign of Christ and of the kind of power He wielded - the power of transformation - as we seek to purify our hearts and “renew a right spirit within us.”

The pine cones are more than ornaments to the evergreen tree. Within them, new seeds are produced. As the wind blows, the pine cone faithfully scatters its seed to produce new life, This is symbolic of what we are to become. After the seed of Christ is implanted in us, the Holy Spirit instructs and prepares us for sowing the seed of the Gospel. If we are faithful in sowing seed, others will experience a new birth in Jesus.

sections.title: The Wreaths
sections.reading:
The most striking and most universal feature of Christmas is the use of these evergreens in churches and homes. A common seasonal use of these evergreens is the wreath. The wreath is a Christian symbol. The circle shape of the wreath stands for eternity, for it has no beginning and no end. God Himself is eternal. It reminds us of life, renewal, and rebirth. Therefore, the Christmas wreath symbolizes the eternal life we, as Christians, find only in Jesus.  He gives us a new life that will never die.

Also, Isaiah tells us that there will be no end to the reign of the Messiah. Therefore, the wreath of evergreens shaped in a circle with no end, also symbolizes the eternal Kingdom of God.

We read in the Scriptures, Isaiah 60:13, “The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my sanctuaries for our Coming King.

As we prepare and “beautify” our sanctuary for the Advent season, may we also prepare and “beautify” our hearts as glorious sanctuaries for our Coming King.
sections.stageInstructions: As Casey & Heather sing those that have been enlisted to do so will hang the wreaths.

sections.title: The Gift of the Candy Cane
sections.reading:
A candy maker in Indiana wanted to make a candy that would be a witness, so he made the Christmas candy cane. He incorporated several symbols for the birth, ministry, and death of Jesus Christ. He began with a stick of pure white, hard candy: white to symbolize the virgin birth and the sinless nature of Jesus, and hard to symbolize the Solid Rock, the foundation of the church and the firmness of the promises of God.

The candy maker made the candy in the form of “J” to represent the precious name of Jesus, who came to earth as our Savior. It could also represent the staff of the Good Shepherd with which He reaches down into the ditches of the world to lift out the fallen lambs who like all sheep have gone astray. Thinking that the candy was somewhat plain, the candy maker stained it with red stripes. He used three small stripes to show the stripes of scourging Jesus received, by which we are healed. The large red stripe was for the blood shed by Christ on the cross so that we could have the promise of eternal life.

The candy became known as the candy cane. Unfortunately, it became a meaningless decoration seen at Christmas time, but the meaning is still there for all those who have “eyes to see and ears to hear.” We pray that this symbol will again be used to witness to the wonder of Jesus and His great love that came down at Christmas. May it be a gift of love that will tell His story - the greatest story ever told.
sections.stageInstructions: The children will now come and give each of you a candy cane as a gift.

sections.title: The Gifts
sections.reading:
From the beginning of Christmas celebrations, gift-giving has been a part of the season. The Wise Men gave out of their treasures, and the Shepherds gave of themselves. Both express the Gift of God in giving Christ as the Savior of the world.

Almost everything we have as part of our celebration can be used as a “bridge” to share with those who do not know Jesus as their Savior. So it is with the gifts of the season. Every time you see a gift, you can remember the gift of the Wise Men, of course, but most importantly the gift of God the Father of His Son to us - the virgin-born, sinless Son of God who was to be the Savior of the world, the most wonderful gift we have ever received. Every time you give a gift or receive a gift or see a gift wrapped it can be a remembrance of the fact that God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, and it can be used as an avenue of sharing about that gift with those who do not know Him or believe in Him.

Our God loves to give us gifts. He blesses us with gifts each day- a sunrise, a new friend, a kind word, family…..James 1:17 says “Every good thing bestowed and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights with whom there is no variation.” God gives us gifts, but His greatest gift was His Son Jesus.

Matthew 2:9-11 says, “ When they had heard the king, they departed; and lo, the star, which they saw in the east, went before them, till it came and stood over where the young child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced with great joy. And when they came into the house, they saw the young child with Mary, his mother, and fell down and worshiped him: and when they had opened their treasures they presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense and myrrh.”
sections.stageInstructions: As Clay plays, the children will place the gifts under the tree.

sections.title: The Poinsettias
sections.reading:
Most Christmas greenery reflects European traditions. But one plant, which looks like a star, the poinsettia, is native to the American continent. It was named after Dr. Joel Robert Poinset, an ambassador to Mexico, who first introduced it to the United States in 1828. The people of Mexico and Central America call this tropical plant the “Flower of the Holy Night”. The star-shaped leaves remind us of Jesus, who was born the infant King. The bracts of the poinsettia are actually leaves, rather than blooms, that turn color. There are several legends surrounding the origin of the poinsettia’s link to Christmas. The most popular is that a poor family had nothing to offer the Christ child at the village church on Christmas Eve. On the way, one of the children picked a bouquet of roadside weeds for the offering and at the altar the leaves turned to the bright green, white, and red of the poinsettia. A more intensely religious interpretation is that the earth responded to the light of the Star of Bethlehem with a reflective plant to shine back in thanks, a star-shaped poinsettia with white leaves. Upon the death of Christ, the white leaves turned red.

The Scriptures say, “Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem, saying, ‘Where is he that is born King of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him.’” Matthew 2:1-2.
sections.stageInstructions: As the music plays, those who have been enlisted will place the poinsettias.

sections.title: The Lighting of the Candles and Christmas Lights
sections.reading:
Christians brought light into the Christmas celebration. They talked about the light of the stars that guided the Wise Men, the light that shed around the angel host, but most of all, that often unread Christmas story in the Gospel of John - the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us - the Light that came into the world.

Light is symbolic of our Lord Jesus Christ who is the Light of the world. He illuminates us from spiritual darkness. Like so, we are to be a light to others, allowing Jesus to shine through us. The custom of placing lighted candles in windows symbolizes a welcome to the Christ child. Ancient legend said that on Christmas Eve, the little Christ child came to earth looking for homes where He might be a guest. Those who would invite Him in set a lighted candle in the window to show Him the way and welcome his coming. The white lights remind us of the pure and unselfish love of God, who gave His only Son for our salvation. The white lights on the Chrismon tree highlight the symbols and remind us of the Providence Baptist families which make up the Body of Christ in this place. As we light the greens and the candles, may we be reminded of the love of our friends and families and of the love of our God who gave His only begotten Son that night.

Jesus spoke saying, “I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.” John 8:12.
sections.stageInstructions: As the congregation sings, those who have been enlisted to do so will come and light our candles and Christmas lights.

sections.title: The Advent Wreath
sections.reading:
The Advent Wreath and its colored candles are the visual focus of the Christmas season. One of the candles is lit each week as Christmas approaches. Advent is a Latin word meaning “the coming”. The Advent Season encompasses the four weeks prior to Christmas. During the season of Advent, Christians prepare for the celebration of the coming of the Lord into the world through the birth of His Son, Jesus Christ. Advent is a time to celebrate light in the midst of darkness.

The circle of the Advent Wreath has no beginning or end. It portrays for us God’s timelessness and His eternal plan. The evergreen represents eternal life that we can have if we accept Him as our Savior. The round shape reminds us of the fellowship of believers around the world who share in the celebration of Jesus’s birth. The candles remind us that the birth of the Light of the world is coming closer.

Our wreath has 5 candles - 3 purple, 1 pink, and 1 white. The purple symbolizes the royalty and Lordship of Jesus and reminds us that Advent is a season of solemn preparation in which we should be spiritually preparing our souls to receive Christ on Christmas. The pink symbolizes an element of rejoicing in the midst of our preparation. The white symbolizes purity and tells us the light of the world is to come. The first candle is purple and is called the Hope or Prophetic candle. The second candle is also purple and is called the Love or Shepherd candle. The third candle is pink and is called the Joy or Angel candle. The fourth candle is purple and is called the Peace or Bethlehem candle. The fifth and last candle is white and is called the Christ candle. The flame will remind us of Jesus’s holiness and purity. It symbolizes Christ who came and gave His life for us so that we might have eternal life.

Tonight, we will light the first candle - the candle of Hope

sections.title: The Lessons of Christmas
sections.reading:
Let us listen to the lessons of the years and the centuries, not just to impressions of the moment. The images of the present in the Biblical story are often discouraging - war, hate, famine, epidemics, a Caesar on his throne, a Paul in prison, Christians being  persecuted. But now, after centuries, the Caesar is gone; Paul is a symbol of faith; and Jesus, the Truth and the Light, is reaching out to every nation!

Let us, through the great traditions of our faith, join with the shepherds of Bethlehem, the wise men from the east, and the seekers throughout the ages, to welcome the One who came at Christmas. Let us at Christmastime bring our gifts to Him, and may the message of our songs be “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth, peace and goodwill to people’s everywhere”.

Let us remember these Christmas symbols and use them to build a bridge to a world that needs to know the gift of God’s Son, Jesus Christ. He has loved us with a love that we can never fully understand but can experience. Let us not go through this season without using every opportunity to share His love that they may be saved.

sections.title: Commision & Blessing
sections.reading:
Bart: Take time, in the busyness of this season, for quiet reflection- for the light of God’s love is discernible everywhere.

Congregation : We will let ourselves be surprised by wonder, and set aside time to offer quiet thanks.

Bart :  The good news of Advent is this: Christ is coming. Christ is always coming.

Congregation : We will welcome Christ into our hearts. We will let ourselves be guided by his ministry. We will go forth from this place in hope.

sections.title: Responsive Reading
sections.reading:
Jimmy Swafford : How shall we prepare this house for the birth of Jesus?

Congregation: With branches of cedar, the tree of excellence and strength.

Jimmy Swafford : How shall we prepare this house for the eternal Christ?

Congregation: With garlands of pine and fir, whose leaves are ever living, evergreen.

Jimmy Swafford : How shall we prepare this house for the prophet of Galilee?

Congregation: With wreaths of holly and ivy, telling of his passion, death, and resurrection.

Jimmy Swafford : How shall we prepare our hearts for this revelation of God?

Congregation: By hearing again the words of the prophets and the promises of God.

Jimmy Swafford : For in the story of Jesus we see revealed the transforming power of God. We are reminded anew of God’s vision of wholeness, justice, and peace for all of creation.

Congregation: Thanks be to God.
